questions.question: Explain the main function of an optical telescope. Distinguish between refracting and reflecting telescopes, and explain why large modern telescopes are reflectors and why bigger telescopes are better.
questions.expected_answer: An optical telescope collects visible light over a large area and focuses it to form a bright image, allowing faint objects to be seen (and magnified). A refracting telescope uses a convex objective lens to refract light to a focus and an eyepiece to magnify (e.g. Galileo's); a reflecting telescope uses a large concave mirror to reflect light to a focus (e.g. Newton's, 1668). Large lenses are heavy, sag and split light into colours, while mirrors can be supported from behind and reflect all colours equally, so large telescopes are reflectors. Light-gathering power depends on area, which increases with the square of diameter (twice the width, four times the light), and larger apertures also give finer detail (resolution).

questions.question: Describe SALT and the Hubble Space Telescope: where each is, the size of its mirror and one advantage of each. Explain why Hubble's images are sharper than those of ground-based telescopes.
questions.expected_answer: SALT (Southern African Large Telescope) is at the South African Astronomical Observatory near Sutherland, Northern Cape, completed 2005; its main mirror is about 11 m by 10 m, made of 91 hexagonal segments each about 1 m across, the largest single optical telescope in the Southern Hemisphere; it collects a huge amount of light, ideal for spectroscopy of faint objects. Hubble was launched in 1990 and orbits about 530 km above Earth (about every 95 minutes) with a 2.4 m mirror. Being above the atmosphere, it avoids the turbulent moving air that bends and blurs starlight (causing twinkling) and can observe ultraviolet and infrared that the atmosphere blocks, so its images are very sharp.

questions.question: Explain how a radio telescope works and why arrays of dishes are used. Give two things radio telescopes can detect that optical telescopes cannot, and describe MeerKAT and the SKA.
questions.expected_answer: A radio telescope uses a large curved metal dish to reflect radio waves (long-wavelength electromagnetic radiation, not sound) to a receiver at the focus, where they are converted into electrical signals analysed by computers. Because radio waves are long, a single dish would need to be enormous for fine detail, so many dishes are linked into an array and their signals combined (interferometry) to act as one huge telescope. Radio waves pass through dust and cloud, so radio telescopes can see the galactic centre and observe day and night; they detect cold hydrogen gas (21 cm), pulsars, black hole jets and the Big Bang afterglow. MeerKAT, in the Karoo near Carnarvon (inaugurated 2018), has 64 dishes each 13.5 m across; it is becoming part of the Square Kilometre Array (SKA), the world's largest radio telescope, with about 200 dishes in South Africa (SKA-Mid) and over 100 000 antennas in Western Australia (SKA-Low), sited in radio-quiet areas protected by law.
